facts.body: Richard Branson of Virgin Records saw an opportunity after major labels rejected the Sex Pistols and signed them in 1977. This "smart move" led to the explosion of the Pistols and punk rock, significantly benefiting Virgin Records. "Branson though saw an opportunity and signed them up. Smart move."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Cancelled Saturday Night Live Appearance (December 17, 1977)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols were originally scheduled to be the special musical guest on Saturday Night Live on December 17, 1977, which was intended to kick off their major North American tour. However, a "major screw up" with obtaining visas led to US customs refusing them entry into the country, prompting SNL to scramble for a replacement and ultimately leading to Elvis Costello's iconic defiant performance. "The special musical guest that night on Saturday Night Live was supposed to have been the sex pistols."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's The Big Deal About Elvis Costello
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Failed Saturday Night Live Debut (1977)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols were scheduled to appear on Saturday Night Live on December 17, 1977, intended as the inaugural event of their first North American tour. However, their appearance was canceled when they encountered issues at immigration, facing scrutiny for improper paperwork and questions related to various criminal charges. "The sex pistols have been booked to appear on Saturday Night Live that week. It was supposed to be the kickoff to their first ever North American tour. But then they got nailed to immigration for improper paperwork and with questions about various criminal charges."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Rolling Stone Magazine Cover (1977)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols were featured on the cover of the October 20th, 1977, edition of Rolling Stone magazine, which carried the headline, "Rock is sick and living in London." This highlights punk's impact and controversy in the late 70s. "The October 20th, 1977 edition of Rolling Stone magazine had the sex pistols on the cover, but the headline, Rock is sick and living in London."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Discovery by Rob Gretton (1977)
facts.body: Rob Gretton, a Manchester punk scene figure and DJ, discovered the band formerly known as Warsaw (now trading as Joy Division) performing at approximately two in the morning as part of a talent showcase in 1977. A mere 20-minute set was enough to fully convince Gretton, who then launched a campaign to become their manager and ultimately secured the job.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Early Sound and Aggression (1977-1978)
facts.body: In their early years, Joy Division's live shows in 1977 and 1978 were characterized by an aggressive, punk-influenced sound. Ian Curtis displayed an aggressive stage presence, and the instrumentation often featured excessive reverberation, contributing to a somewhat "contaminated" sound, reflecting a preference for first takes. "Cuando vemos los conciertos que había dado Joy Division posiblemente en los primeros años, 77, 78, seguían siendo una banda bastante agresiva, vemos ahí en Cortis Cantardo, una muy agresiva, vemos esa reverberación excesiva a veces de los instrumentos, vemos esa contaminación que hace que no llegue a Sprite a la ende nada, en claro, es amor por las primeras tomas que los iba a grabar tan rápido."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 2. Unknown Pleasures
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Early Career and Rise to Stardom (1977-1988)
facts.body: Depeche Mode formed between 1977 and 1980, developing a synth-based approach that was trendy at the time. For about six years, they maintained a mid-level status with a cult following until their sixth album, "Music for the Masses," released in 1987, propelled them to superstardom with global hit singles. "Depeche Mode came together between 1977 and 1980."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour

facts.title: Keith Richards' 1977 Drug Arrest and Trial
facts.body: Keith Richards was significantly less involved in the creation of "Some Girls" because, in 1977, he experienced a severe drug relapse. He was facing a drug possession trial in Canada, which required him to travel frequently for declarations, making him largely unavailable for the album's composition, which Mick Jagger mostly handled. "Richard trabajó muy poco en el álbum, porque el año anterior en 1977 había tenido un revá con las drogas, estaba pendiente de un juicio, a dor posicion de Rolling Stones, en Canadá."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: The Rolling Stones: Some Girls y su portada llena de demandas.

facts.title: Third Cycle (1977-Mid-1984)
facts.body: A reaction to the "mediocrities of the early 1970s," this cycle began with the rise of punk rock, specifically highlighted by the Sex Pistols' contract signing on March 10, 1977. Punk and New Wave helped pave the way for the music video generation before rock "blown itself out" by mid-1984. "The third cycle was a reaction to the mediocrities of the early 1970s, fed up with the state of music, a new generation embraced punk rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14
facts.name: Rock & Roll

facts.title: Evolution into Funk and Soul (Pre-1977)
facts.body: Before 1977, R&B had already started evolving, giving rise to various forms of funk and soul music, as well as different types of dance music. This diversification laid the groundwork for further genre splits. "R&B began to begat things like funk in various forms of soul and dance music."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)
facts.name: r&b

facts.title: Split Leading to Disco (1977)
facts.body: The year 1977 was pivotal for R&B, leading to a significant split that resulted in the emergence of disco. This new genre brought a lot of polarization within popular music but ultimately left an "incredible" legacy. "On the R&B side, we got disco."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)
facts.name: r&b

facts.title: Major Type of Popular Music (Pre-1977)
facts.body: Prior to 1977, R&B was considered one of the few major types of popular music, alongside pop, rock, and country, under which all music could be broadly grouped. "Up until about 1977 there were only a few major types of popular music. You had pop, you had rock, you had country, and R&B."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: The Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Performance in 1977 was won by Aretha Franklin for "Master of Eyes," over Diana Ross's "Love Hangover." "love hangover was nominated for a Grammy for best female R&B performance but lost to master of eyes by a wreath of Franklin."

facts.title: Arrested for Stealing a Pillowcase and Towels – Newcastle, June 1977, Fined 100 Pounds
facts.body: On June 11, 1977, Joe Strummer and Topper Headon were in Newcastle. The following night they were arrested on robbery charges for allegedly stealing a pillowcase and several towels from a Holiday Inn. They were supposed to have appeared in court in May 1977 to answer these charges but had simply not turned up. A judge took a dim view of the non-appearance; in the end they were fined 100 pounds each. "I mean, the Clash. They were arrested for stealing a pillowcase."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 7
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Controversial Major Label Signing (1977)
facts.body: On January 26, 1977, The Clash signed a significant record deal with CBS, a major multinational corporation. This deal, valued at 100,000 pounds (reportedly 75,000 pounds higher than competing offers), sparked outrage and accusations of "sell out" from their fans across the UK. Despite being perceived as uncompromisingly socialist and anti-establishment, the band maintained they aimed to "corrupt the music industry from within." "The day the clash allegedly sold out January 26, 1977."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: CBS Records Contract (1977)
facts.body: On January 25, 1977, The Clash signed a worldwide recording contract with CBS Records for 100,000 pounds. This occurred at the height of punk rock in the UK. The deal sparked outrage among other punk bands and fans, who viewed it as a betrayal of their anti-capitalist, populist punk rebel image. The fanzine Stephen Glue even declared "punk died the day the clash signed to CBS." "And on January 25, 1977, at the very height of punk rock in the UK, they signed a worldwide recording contract with CBS records for 100,000 pounds."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Record Deal with CBS (1977)
facts.body: The Clash signed a record deal with CBS on January 25, 1977, and subsequently began preparations for their first album. "As far as British punk went, the clash finally signed a record deal with CBS on the 25th."

facts.title: Term Coined in 1977
facts.body: The term "post punk" emerged around 1977, coinciding with the peak of punk, to describe the music that came after it. It served as an umbrella term for a new sound that rejected traditional rock and roll norms but maintained a connection to punk's expressive freedom. "Ergo, the name post punk, which was an umbrella term for this music."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: Emergence in 1977
facts.body: The year 1977 is considered the beginning of post-punk, alongside punk rock and New Wave, marking a significant shift in music after the earlier prolific years of rock. "1977 punk, the beginning of New Wave, the era of post punk and all that came with it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Amazing Year That Was 1991
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: Frenetic Birth and Diversification (1977-1981)
facts.body: The period from 1977 to 1981 was exceptionally frenetic in music history, witnessing the birth and ramification of numerous genres. Within this rapid diversification, Post-Punk emerged, with Joy Division's first album, *Unknown Pleasures*, considered a potential culmination and significant origin point for the genre. "Dentro de todo ese cúmulo de ramificaciones nace la semi del POSPANG y posiblemente el gran germen del POSPANG, es el primer disco de J-Division."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 2. Unknown Pleasures

facts.title: I Feel Love (1977) as Futuristic Disco
facts.body: Donna Summer's "I Feel Love," produced by Giorgio Moroder in 1977, was a significant disco album, yet it distinguished itself with a "robotic, futuristic" sound. This innovative approach, driven by Moroder's experimentation with synthesizers, made it extremely inspirational for those exploring electronic music. "The album was disco, but it was different, robotic, futuristic, and those who were into experimenting with synths found it to be extremely inspirational."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Emergence from R&B (1977)
facts.body: Disco emerged as a significant new genre from R&B in 1977, following a "big split" in musical styles. Its appearance led to considerable polarization but ultimately established an "incredible" and lasting legacy. "On the R&B side, we got disco."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Dominance in Post-1977 Era
facts.body: Following the punk and new wave era, disco, pop, and hair metal dominated a "long follow period," which, while popular, was not seen as music that changed the world. "lots of disco, lots of pop, lots of hair metal, which was great if you were into that kind of thing, but not exactly music that changed the world"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Amazing Year That Was 1991
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Dominance in 1977
facts.body: Disco became the "king" of both the dance floor and radio in 1977, dramatically sweeping over the music industry "like a tidal wave" and significantly impacting the visibility and success of other genres like reggae. "My theory on this is very simple disco disco was king not just on the dance floor, but on the radio in 1977 it came over the music industry like a title wave."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Joining Sex Pistols as Bassist – February 1977
facts.body: After Glenn Matlock was fired from the Sex Pistols in February 1977, manager Malcolm McLaren decided to replace him with a fan. Sid was chosen because he was always around and was Johnny Rotten's friend, embodying the punk ethos of the ultimate fan joining the ultimate band. "Malcolm McLaren came up with the idea of hiring one of the group's fans as his replacement."

facts.body: Psychedelic rock, referred to as "psych," was identified as one of the multitude of different directions that rock music had grown into by 1977, signifying an early and distinct subgenre within the broader rock landscape. "Rock had already grown in a multitude of different directions, metal, Prague, psych, and the so-called corporate rock bands like Boston and Kansas."

facts.title: Influential After 1977
facts.body: Kraftwerk is considered by some to be the most influential band in the world next to The Beatles, with their impact traceable in music starting anytime after 1977. Their influence spans EDM, techno (including Detroit techno and Daft Punk), ambient and chillout music, synth and sample-constructed music (like Simple Minds and Depeche Mode), early 80s techno pop (OMD, Soft Cell), and industrial music (Nine Inch Nails). "Pick any starting point in music anytime after 1977. And you will somehow be led back in some fashion to Craftwork."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: 1977 British Context
facts.body: In 1977, reggae was not as ubiquitous as it is today; its growing popularity in Britain was spurred by the political and economic situation in Jamaica, which led many Jamaicans to immigrate to Britain under a soon-to-be-eliminated Commonwealth law. "Ari developed a taste for reggae. And this is more radical than it sounds right now. See today, reggae and scott, that's everywhere, right? Not so in 1977, but that was changing thanks to the political and economic situation in Jamaica."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7
facts.name: Reggae

facts.title: Disco's Impact (1977)
facts.body: The overwhelming dominance of disco in 1977, both in dance clubs and on radio, swept over the music industry "like a tidal wave" and significantly hampered reggae's ability to achieve mainstream success in the American market. "My theory on this is very simple disco disco was king not just on the dance floor, but on the radio in 1977 it came over the music industry like a title wave. And reggae did not stand much of a chance."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

"My theory on this is very simple disco disco was king not just on the dance floor, but on the radio in 1977 it came over the music industry like a title wave. And reggae did not stand much of a chance."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 29 - Every Little Thing is Gonna Be All Right - The Influence of 70s Reggae
facts.name: Reggae

"on album rock radio almost every song on the album became an FM staple from the chain to second hand news to Gold Dust Woman."

facts.title: My Aim Is True (1977) – Debut Album Recorded by Clover, Who Became Huey Lewis and the News
facts.body: Before his music career, Elvis Costello worked as a computer operator for Elizabeth Arden cosmetics, running invoices on an IBM 360 mainframe, taking occasional sick days to demo songs. When he signed to Stiff Records, he needed a backing band. An American group called Clover had just arrived in England hoping for their big break, but found themselves stranded in the middle of punk and unwanted. They needed money for plane tickets home. Elvis went to their residency at Headley Grange, told them he needed a studio band and specifically didn't need a singer, so Clover's own singer was sent to wait elsewhere while the rest of the band backed Elvis through six four-hour sessions for his debut. Clover was paid and sent back to the US, where they reinvented themselves as Huey Lewis and the News. The singer who had to hang out during the Costello sessions was Huey Lewis. "That banished singer was Huey Lewis."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 6
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.title: "Nerd Rock" Attribution and SNL Sketches (December 1977)
facts.body: During his appearance on Saturday Night Live in December 1977, Elvis Costello, characterized by his thick glasses and powder-blue sport coat, was performing at the peak of his "angry young songwriter" phase. A writer for the show, Beats, observed his performance and coined the term "nerd rock" to describe his style, leading to the creation of the recurring "Nerds" sketches on SNL featuring Gilda Radner, Jane Curtin, and Bill Murray. "this isn't punk rock, this is nerd rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: History of Nerd Rock
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.title: Saturday Night Live Appearance (December 1977)
facts.body: During his performance on Saturday Night Live in December 1977, at the peak of his "angry young songwriter" phase, Elvis Costello, dressed with thick glasses and a powder blue sport coat, was observed by SNL writer Tom Davis, who famously thought, "this isn't punk rock, this is nerd rock." This moment contributed to the coining of the term "nerd rock" and directly led to the creation of the recurring "The Nerds" sketch on the show. "In December 1977, Elvis Costello appeared on Saturday Night Live. He was at the height of his angry young songwriter years, complete with his thick glasses and powder blue sport coat."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Nerd Rock
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.body: Elvis Costello's music from 1977 is referenced as a starting point for discussions on the post-punk era, indicating his early presence in the evolving music landscape. "a little oldest Costello from 1977 to start things."

facts.title: Saturday Night Live Act of Defiance (December 17, 1977)
facts.body: Elvis Costello's North American breakthrough came when he was a last-minute replacement musical guest on Saturday Night Live on December 17, 1977, after the Sex Pistols faced visa issues. NBC insisted he play his British hit "Less Than Zero" and avoid "Radio, Radio," which was critical of radio (a sensitive topic given NBC's radio station ownership). Costello feigned agreement but defiantly launched into "Radio, Radio" live on air, an "act of corporate nose thumming" that inspired thousands. "That act of defiance, that act of corporate nose thumming inspired thousands."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's The Big Deal About Elvis Costello
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.title: Prolific Output and Market Dilution (1977-1986)
facts.body: Costello released a new album every year between 1977 and 1986, a rate considered "too prolific." This rapid creation of new music meant his labels often lacked sufficient time to promote and market his albums effectively, and the music press struggled to keep up with reviews. The "glut of material" ultimately diluted his market worth and equity, even among diehard fans. "Elvis released a new album every year between 1977 and 1986."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's The Big Deal About Elvis Costello
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.title: Saturday Night Live Stunt (1977)
facts.body: Costello and The Attractions secured their appearance on NBC TV's *Saturday Night Live* only because the original guests, The Sex Pistols, were unable to perform due to visa issues. Columbia Records insisted Costello perform his single "Less Than Zero," but believing Americans wouldn't understand its subject matter (British fascist Oswald Mosley), Costello abruptly stopped the song after just seven seconds live on the air and switched to the then-unreleased "Radio, Radio." This act enraged SNL producer Lorne Michaels and NBC brass, leading to Costello being banned from the show for a dozen years. However, Columbia Records viewed it as excellent publicity, solidifying Costello's image as a "punk fellow traveler" and an "actual angry young man." "What Costello pulled live on the air that night became the stuff of legend."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 1
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.title: Formation and Sound (1977)
facts.body: When The Police emerged in 1977, their sound was unique, blending punky elements with pop sensibilities and an unusual reggae influence for the time. "When the police first showed up in 1977, they sounded like no one else. They were punky but tempered with pop. And they had this reggae thing going which was highly unusual for the day."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt-Rocks Great Bass Players
facts.name: The Police

facts.title: 1977 Breakthrough Sound
facts.body: When The Police emerged in 1977, Stuart Copeland's drumming immediately distinguished itself from other New Wave drummers of the era. His snare drum was tuned very tightly, producing a sharp, high-pitched crack, and his playing incorporated a distinct reggae and dub feel, often expressed with rim shots. There was also a subtle Middle Eastern infusion blended with jazz, evident in his use of small, high-pitched splash cymbals, making him one of the first modern rock drummers to adopt them. He was also notable for his syncopated beats led from the hi-hat. "When they came along in 1977, he immediately stood out from all the other new wave drummers of the era."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit
facts.name: The Police

facts.title: Productive Partnership with Bowie (1977)
facts.body: The unexpected success of "Low" solidified a fantastic and highly productive partnership between David Bowie and Brian Eno throughout 1977, leading to a period of intense creativity and projection for the Berlin Trilogy. However, this close relationship began to wane after "Heroes," with less harmony in subsequent projects.

facts.title: Role on Heroes (1977)
facts.body: Brian Eno was heavily credited for his work on "Heroes," appearing on almost the entire album. His influence was particularly evident in the second, largely instrumental, side of the album, which strongly resembled his solo projects and collaborations with artists like Cluster from the late 1970s.

facts.title: Digital Recording and Optical Disk Development (1977-1978)
facts.body: In Japan, Sony was actively developing digital recording machines and first showcased a 30-centimeter optical disk (the same diameter as a vinyl LP) in September 1977, capable of holding 60 minutes of music. A year later, they advanced this to a disk holding up to 150 minutes, still at 30 centimeters. "Meanwhile, in Japan, Sony was working on digital recording machines and first demonstrated an optical disk that was 30 centimeters in diameter. So the same diameter as a vinyl LP, one foot. This was September 1977."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Sex Pistols Payoff (1977)
facts.body: EMI Records paid the Sex Pistols 40,000 pounds in 1977 to terminate their contract and effectively make them "go away." This occurred just before the band signed a new deal with A&M Records, highlighting the controversial nature of the Sex Pistols and the desire of established labels to distance themselves from the band's antics. "After being paid 40,000 pounds to go away by EMI records..."

facts.title: Dropping The Sex Pistols (1977)
facts.body: After the Sex Pistols' notorious TV appearance and alleged public misbehavior, EMI found the band too "toxic" and "just couldn't take it anymore," paying them £40,000 to terminate their contract in early 1977. "But the bottom line here is that EMI, home of the Beatles, and the owners of Abbey Road recording studios just couldn't take it anymore."

facts.title: News of the World (1977) - Album Cover Iconography
facts.body: The iconic robot on the "News of the World" album cover is a nearly identical copy of a sci-fi fanzine from 1953. The original artist from the fanzine was commissioned by the band to create the cover, and also developed all the iconography within the album, including original paintings in the booklet depicting people screaming in terror from the robot, and related posters. This visual has been highly influential, inspiring reinterpretations in comics like X-Men and even a subtle nod in a Family Guy episode. "Realmente es una copia casi idéntica de un fancine de ciencia afición de 1953."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica
facts.name: Queen

facts.title: Founding and Location (1977)
facts.body: The Power Station, located in New York at approximately 53rd and 10th, was founded in 1977 by Tony Bongiovi, the second cousin of John Bon Jovi. The building previously served as a Consolidated Edison power plant and later a TV studio for "Let's Make a Deal." "In 1977, the building was bought and rebuilt as a recording studio by Tony Bongeovi, the second cousin of some New Jersey kid named John Bongeovi."

facts.title: Evolution Post-1977
facts.body: Following the traditional heyday, bands like 38 Special evolved their sound to be more commercially viable, seeking radio play and MTV exposure. Donnie Van Zant even declared the term "Southern Rock" passé in 1986, indicating a deliberate move away from the genre's stereotypical imagery towards "arena rock." "I think that hold on loosely sounds a lot more like a Rainer Rock than Southern Rock, which seems to be what 38 Special thought they needed to do to sell more records."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.body: Quincy Jones was invited by author Alex Haley to score the televised adaptation of Haley's acclaimed novel of African American history, *Roots*. The epic 1977 miniseries garnered the highest TV ratings ever recorded to that date, and the project earned Quincy Jones his first Emmy award for his musical contribution. "As for his own recordings, Quincy was invited by the author Alex Haley to score the televised adaptation of Roots, his acclaimed novel of African American History."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Convair Plane Crash (1977)
facts.body: On October 20, 1977, a Convair twin-engine prop plane carrying members of Lynyrd Skynyrd ran out of fuel near Gillsburg, Mississippi, and subsequently went down in a swamp. Three members of the band were tragically killed in the crash. "October 20th, 1977, a Converter twin-engine prop ran out of fuel to your Gillsburg, Mississippi, and went down in a swamp. Three members of Leonard Skinnerd were killed in the crash."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Airplanes!
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: Plane Crash (1977)
facts.body: In 1977, a plane crash tragically killed Ronny Van Zant and two other members of Lynyrd Skynyrd. This event is often cited by fans and critics as the point at which "Southern Rock lost its edge," marking the end of its heyday. "after the plane crash that killed Ronnie Van Zant and two other members of Leonard Skinnerd that Southern Rock lost its edge. 1977 was the end of Southern Rock, they say."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 3 - Nostalgia, Race, and Rebels in 70s Southern Rock (Encore)
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: 1977 Plane Crash
facts.body: Ronnie Van Zant, along with two other members of the band, died in an awful plane crash in 1977. This tragic event is often cited by fans as the moment when Southern Rock lost its edge and marked the end of its heyday. "Ronnie Van Zantt was responding to Neil Young song Southern man."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Engine Failures and Emergency Communication (October 20, 1977)
facts.body: Around 6:40 PM, roughly halfway through the trip, the right engine, which had sounded problematic from the start, sputtered and died. At 6:42 PM, Captain McCurray contacted Houston Air Route Traffic Control, requesting the closest airport, and was directed to McCone Pike County Airport in McCone, Mississippi, about 17 kilometers behind them. Before the plane could turn, the left engine also failed, rendering hydraulics and steering inoperative. "Around halfway through the trip, at 6.40pm, the right engine, which didn't sound good to begin with, spotted and then died."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing...Uncharted: The Lynyrd Skynyrd Plane Crash
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: Final Flight Details (October 20, 1977)
facts.body: The Convair took off from Greenville at 5:02 PM Eastern Time on October 20, 1977, with 22 passengers, Captain McCurray, and First Officer Gray. They climbed to a cruising altitude of 12,000 feet for the approximately three-hour flight to Baton Rouge, initially carrying 5.5 hours' worth of fuel. "The Convair took off from Greenville at 502 Eastern Time, with 22 passengers and Captain McCurry and first officer Gray at the controls."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing...Uncharted: The Lynyrd Skynyrd Plane Crash
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: In-flight Engine Incident (October 18, 1977)
facts.body: On October 18, 1977, during a flight from Lakeland, Florida, to Greenville, the right engine of the Convair 240 shot out ten-foot flames at an altitude of 12,000 feet for several minutes. This alarming event led to the band's decision to ditch the Convair for a brand new Learjet upon reaching Baton Rouge for their October 20 gig at Louisiana State University. "On October 18th, the band flew into Greenville from Lakeland, Florida. At one point, ten-foot flames shot out of the right engine at an altitude of 12,000 feet for several minutes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing...Uncharted: The Lynyrd Skynyrd Plane Crash
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: Last Concert and Tour Plans (October 1977)
facts.body: The next leg of their tour commenced on October 13 in Statesboro, Georgia. The band had ambitious plans to play Madison Square Garden several weeks later, a long-held dream. Their final performance before the crash was on October 19, 1977, at the Greenville Memorial Auditorium in Greenville, South Carolina. "The next leg of the tour began on October 13th in statesboro, Georgia, and would eventually see the band realize their dreams by playing Madison Square Garden several weeks down the road."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing...Uncharted: The Lynyrd Skynyrd Plane Crash
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: Plane Crash (October 20, 1977)
facts.body: At 6:52 PM, the Convair 240 carrying Leonard Skinnerd and a significant portion of their crew crashed into a forest near the Mississippi-Louisiana border, 60 miles from Baton Rouge, which should have been only ten minutes away. The plane, traveling at approximately 200 miles an hour, cut a 500-foot swathe through pine trees before splitting into three pieces—the cockpit and tail ripping away—and coming to a stop at 6:53 PM in a snake-infested mangrove swamp. "At 6.52pm, the Conveyor 240 carrying Leonard Skinnerd in a big chunk of their crew descended into a forest close to the Mississippi Louisiana border, 60 miles from Baton Rouge."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing...Uncharted: The Lynyrd Skynyrd Plane Crash
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: Toe Injury Leading to Cancer (May 1977)
facts.body: On May 9, 1977, in Paris, while playing soccer with bandmates between gigs, Bob Marley injured his big right toe when a French journalist wearing spikes stepped on it. This toe had been previously injured multiple times (by broken glass, a rock, almost cut off) and consistently struggled to heal, becoming a recurring issue. "One of the people he was playing with was a French journalist, and he was wearing spikes, and that guy stepped on Bob's foot. He injured his big right toe, and it didn't really seem to want to heal."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1
facts.name: Bob Marley

facts.title: Acral Lentiginous Melanoma Diagnosis and Refusal of Amputation (July 1977)
facts.body: In July 1977, a doctor in London diagnosed Bob Marley with acral lentiginous melanoma, a rare form of skin cancer discovered under his toenail that was not well documented in medical texts at the time. Despite the doctors' advice for toe amputation, Marley refused, citing his Rastafarian belief that removing any body part would be a sin, opting instead for a skin graft from his thigh performed by a Miami specialist. "In July, he visited a doctor in London, and they discovered he had something called Acro-leteginus melanoma, a pre-existing form of skin cancer under the nail that at the time wasn't well covered in the medical textbooks." "But Bob refused, saying that as a rastifarian, it would be a sin to have any body part removed."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1
facts.name: Bob Marley

facts.title: Impact of "I Feel Love" on Gay Clubs (1977)
facts.body: "I Feel Love" became a significant smash in discos, particularly within gay clubs, where its innovative sound and ecstatic vocals resonated strongly. "The record was a smash in discos, particularly Reynolds notes, gay clubs, and artists from Blondie to the human league to David Bowie and Brian Eno took inspiration from it."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: The Queen of Disco Edition Part 1 (Encore)
facts.name: Donna Summer

facts.title: Chart Success Amidst Disco's Rise (1977)
facts.body: By November 1977, when "I Feel Love" peaked on the Hot 100, disco was rapidly dominating charts across America and Europe, with the film *Saturday Night Fever* opening the following month, solidifying Summer's status as a consistent international hitmaker. "By the time I Feel Love reached its peak on the Hot 100 in November 1977, disco was taking over the charts in both America and Europe. Saturday Night Fever would open in movie theaters the next month, and Summer became a more consistent hitmaker on both sides of the Atlantic."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: The Queen of Disco Edition Part 1 (Encore)

facts.title: Roger Moore Era Bond Themes (1977-1983)
facts.body: Several James Bond themes during the Roger Moore era, including Carly Simon's "Nobody Does It Better" (1977), Shirley Bassey's "Moonraker" (1979), Sheena Easton's "For Your Eyes Only" (1981), and Rita Coolidge's "All Time High" (1983), adopted a "very mature adult contemporary" sound. These themes were seen as fitting Moore's "joky" portrayal of Bond better than rock songs. "All very mature adult contemporary you know. Maybe all these songs fit Roger Moore's bonds and the tone of those films a lot better than a rock song."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: First Wave (1977-mid 1980) – Cold and Robotic
facts.body: This initial period was characterized by a cold, robotic musical approach, laying the foundational groundwork for what would later be known as industrial music. "The first was from 1977 through to about the middle of 1980. That was when the cold, robotic approach was invoked. Songs like this formed the very basic foundations of what we would later call industrial music."

"Firefall is not country. I think today the kids would call it Yacht Rock, I think."

facts.title: Opening for Peter Gabriel (1977)
facts.body: Following the critical success of *Marquee Moon*, Television opened for Peter Gabriel in 1977. This pairing, however, was not successful, as Television fans found Gabriel's theatrics excessive, while Gabriel's fans considered Television "cold and distant," highlighting a clash between two different rock genres. "Television fans thought that Gabriel's theatrics were too much and Gabriel's fans thought that television was cold and distant."

facts.title: Pioneering "New Wave" Marketing (Early 1977)
facts.body: Sire Records invented the term "New Wave" as a marketing strategy in early 1977, launching a campaign called "Don't Call it Punk." This aimed to re-brand British punk rock into a more palatable and commercially viable genre for the North American market, fostering new opportunities for bands like The Pretenders, Depeche Mode, Elvis Costello, Echo & the Bunnymen, The Cure, and The Smiths. "And before the company was bought by Warner and ceased to be an indie label, someone in the office invented a new term."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1
facts.name: Sire Records

facts.title: First "New Wave" Compilation (1977)
facts.body: Sire Records (referred to as "Fono Grande de Estados Unidos") released what is noted as almost the first compilation album titled "New Wave" in 1977. This album was a "catch-all" that included a diverse mix of artists such as Ramones, Talking Heads, and The Residents, highlighting the early, diffuse nature of the New Wave movement. "la discográfica de la Fono Grande de Estados Unidos en el 77 se acabó un recopilatorio llamado New Wave casi el primer recopilatorio que se llama New Wave, y que es un cajón de sáster donde está todo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Que es el New Wave
facts.name: Sire Records

facts.title: Sex Pistols Contract and Termination (March 1977)
facts.body: A&M Records signed the Sex Pistols to a 150,000-pound deal on March 10, 1977, in front of Buckingham Palace in London, only to drop them six days later. The termination was prompted by the band's extensive trashing of the A&M offices after the signing and negative feedback from other artists on the label, such as Captain & Tennille. Despite the termination, the Sex Pistols still walked away with 75,000 pounds. "Six days later, ANM announced that they were dropping the band in part due to the flak they were getting from other acts on the label, acts like the captain and tenel."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: A&M Records

facts.title: Sex Pistols Signing Incident – March 10, 1977
facts.body: The Sex Pistols signed their record deal with A&M Records outside Buckingham Palace on March 10, 1977. This event was a significant moment in the band's history before their notoriously brief and tumultuous career. "Sid really got into being a sex pistol. He was there when the pistol signed their record deal with A&M records outside of Buckingham Palace in March 10th, 1977."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: A&M Records

facts.title: Sex Pistols "God Save the Queen" Release and Destruction (1977)
facts.body: A&M Records signed the Sex Pistols for a mere five days in 1977, during which time approximately 25,000 copies of their "God Save the Queen" 7-inch single were pressed. Following the band's dismissal due to other artists' objections, these singles were ordered destroyed, though several dozen were "liberated" and became highly valuable collectibles. "But in that five days, A&M had pressed up something like 25,000 copies of God Save the Queen."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2
facts.name: A&M Records

facts.title: Brief Sex Pistols Contract (1977)
facts.body: Two months after the Sex Pistols were dropped by EMI, A&M Records decided to take a chance and signed them. However, a party at the label's offices following the signing resulted in significant damage, and complaints from other A&M artists like The Carpenters, along with questions from head office in Los Angeles, led to the band being dropped after just six days, with a £75,000 buyout. "Two months later, an M records decided to take a chance and signed the pistols to another deal."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: A&M Records

facts.title: Brief Sex Pistols Signing (1977)
facts.body: In early 1977, A&M Records signed the Sex Pistols after EMI dropped them, but the deal lasted only five days due to rebellion from other A&M artists who refused to be on the same label as the "Yabos," leading management to drop the band. "After being dropped by EMI records because of their bad behavior, they were picked up by A&M records. And that deal lasted for a total of five days."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Valuable Vinyl
facts.name: A&M Records

facts.title: Destruction Order for "God Save the Queen" (1977)
facts.body: Following the termination of their contract with the Sex Pistols in 1977, A&M Records ordered the pressing plant to destroy all 25,000 copies of the "God Save the Queen" 7-inch single that had been pressed on the A&M label. "When that contract was terminated, A&M ordered the pressing plant to destroy any and all copies of the God saved the queen seven inch that had been pressed up on A&M records."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
